changes.title: At home after treatment
changes.before: Follow individual instructions on distance and time with other people, sleeping arrangements, toilets, body fluids, laundry, work and transport. Restrictions may extend to three weeks for some contacts. Contact the medical physicist before discharge if you cannot follow the plan at home.
changes.after: Before discharge, obtain a paper plan with the end date for each restriction on contact, sleeping, work, travel and body-fluid handling. First-week instructions include daily bathing, careful handwashing, sitting to pass urine and separately washing body-fluid-soiled laundry. Ask for specific advice about pads, incontinence or a catheter. Examples include sleeping separately from a partner for 14 days and from pregnant people or children for three weeks; restrictions differ by contact and circumstance. Your medical physicist sets your personal instructions. Tell them before discharge if you cannot follow the plan at home.

chapter.title: Your PRRT course
chapter.intro: Receptor-directed radiation with specialist safety checks.

items.title: Why PRRT?
items.text: PRRT carries radiation to somatostatin receptors on NET cells to help control disease that cannot be removed or has spread. A specialist NET and nuclear-medicine team checks receptor imaging, organ function and your priorities before recommending it.

items.title: How it works
items.text: Lutathera joins a receptor-binding molecule to the radioactive element lutetium-177. After infusion, it attaches to somatostatin receptors on suitable NET cells and delivers radiation nearby. The receptor scan helps select patients. Kidneys and blood-forming marrow can also receive radiation, which is why kidney protection and long-term blood monitoring matter.

items.title: Why the amino acids matter
items.text: The amino-acid infusion reduces the amount of radioactive medicine retained in the kidneys. It is an essential part of kidney protection. It can cause nausea and affect potassium or fluid balance, so anti-sickness treatment, blood tests and observation are needed.

items.title: Four intended administrations
items.text: Four administrations are planned, usually eight weeks apart. Lutathera is infused over about 30–40 minutes, with a four-hour kidney-protective amino-acid infusion and anti-sickness treatment. The visit is much longer than the Lutathera infusion; an overnight stay may be needed.

items.title: Evidence and its limits
items.text: Lutetium-177 DOTATATE with standard-dose octreotide improved time before progression compared with high-dose octreotide. The final overall-survival comparison was not statistically significant. The findings do not promise a survival gain for an individual. NETTER-1 was a midgut study. Its results must not be presented as identical evidence for every pancreatic, other GI or grade 3 NET. Your specialist team confirms that the treatment criteria apply to you.

chapter.title: Preparing for hospital and returning home
chapter.intro: The service supplies a personal written plan.

items.title: Before admission
items.text: Confirm SSTR imaging, appointments, recent bloods, hormone medicines and pregnancy precautions. Tell the team about kidney/heart problems, incontinence, a catheter, childcare or close contact with pregnant people; these may change the practical plan.

items.title: Treatment day
items.text: The standard NCCP activity is 7.4 GBq by intravenous infusion, usually every eight weeks for four administrations; the specialist may alter, delay or stop treatment. Lutathera runs over approximately 30–40 minutes. A lysine/arginine amino-acid infusion starts 30 minutes beforehand and continues for four hours. An anti-sickness medicine is given at least 30 minutes before the amino acids. The first visit generally includes an overnight stay; later treatments may be day case or overnight. The service confirms your plan.

items.title: SSA injections: stop and restart
items.text: The NET and nuclear-medicine teams must coordinate the injection plan. Do not translate “about four weeks” into your own date: NCCP specifies 30 days for long-acting SSA and 24 hours for short-acting SSA before PRRT. Restart timing follows the written service plan; it can differ with day-case arrangements.

items.title: At home after treatment
items.text: Follow individual instructions on distance and time with other people, sleeping arrangements, toilets, body fluids, laundry, work and transport. Restrictions may extend to three weeks for some contacts. Contact the medical physicist before discharge if you cannot follow the plan at home.

items.title: Travel and other healthcare
items.text: Carry the discharge letter and treatment card, including the date and type of radioactive treatment. Ask about travel and radiation detectors. Tell any healthcare staff you have had PRRT; urgent care must never be delayed because of radiation precautions.

chapter_items.title: The full safety-test sequence
chapter_items.text: Baseline blood count, kidneys/liver, ECHO/MUGA and pregnancy assessment where applicable. Counts/kidneys/liver once 2–4 weeks before and shortly before each infusion, every two weeks between, then every four weeks for at least three months after the final dose and every three months for the following year. Potassium is checked before amino acids. Renal monitoring continues at least through the first year. Post-infusion radiation scans and response scans have separate purposes.

chapter_items.title: What may change treatment
chapter_items.text: The specialist may postpone, reduce or stop treatment for low counts, kidney/liver abnormalities, other toxicity or disease change. A four-stamp record shows intended administrations; it cannot confirm medical suitability.

chapter_items.title: Post-treatment scans
chapter_items.text: Your specialist team plans special scans after each infusion to measure radiation delivered to organs. CT/MRI or other scans to assess tumour response follow the specialist plan.

chapter_items.title: When to seek help
chapter_items.text: Seek urgent help for sudden severe flushing with faintness, severe diarrhoea, wheeze or breathing trouble, especially in the first 48 hours; follow the hormone-crisis plan. Fever, bleeding, much less urine, persistent severe abdominal pain, muscle weakness or confusion needs prompt advice. Tell emergency staff when you received PRRT; radiation precautions must not delay urgent care.

chapter_items.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
chapter_items.text: Lutathera can harm an unborn child and may affect fertility. Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Use effective contraception during treatment and for seven months after the last dose for patients who could become pregnant; men with partners who could become pregnant need contraception during treatment and for four months afterwards. Breastfeeding must stop before treatment; follow specialist advice.

chapter_items.title: If a visit is delayed
chapter_items.text: The team decides whether a delayed administration remains suitable and whether activity must change. Do not assume a treatment can automatically proceed at the maximum interval. Continue the blood-test and symptom plan.

chapter_items.title: Contacts and paperwork
chapter_items.text: Write the actual NET, PRRT nursing and radiation-protection contacts on the paper plan. Example numbers are not clinical contact lines. Keep the written precautions and urgent hormone-symptom instructions with the discharge letter.
